Seven SRFI libraries, **173 new names**, each with a reference
page under [`docs/srfi/`](https://github.com/MrXie1109/GoScheme/tree/main/docs/srfi),
plus a bilingual guide under
[`docs/manual/`](https://github.com/MrXie1109/GoScheme/tree/main/docs/manual).

| Library | Names | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `(srfi 1)` | 97 | the list library: `fold`, `unfold`, `reduce`, `take-while`, `span`, `delete-duplicates`, `lset-*` and the rest |
| `(srfi 2)` | 1 | `and-let*` |
| `(srfi 8)` | 1 | `receive` |
| `(srfi 26)` | 2 | `cut` and `cute` |
| `(srfi 111)` | 4 | `box`, `unbox`, `set-box!`, `box?` |
| `(srfi 128)` | 30 | comparators, with `hash-bound`/`hash-salt` as parameters |
| `(srfi 133)` | 38 | the vector library |

```scheme
(import (scheme base) (srfi 1) (srfi 26) (srfi 8) (srfi 128) (srfi 133))

(receive (q r) (floor/ 7 2) (list q r))        ; => (3 1)
(map (cut * 2 <>) '(1 2 3))                    ; => (2 4 6)
(fold - 0 '(1 2 3))                            ; => 2   (SRFI-1 argument order)
(lset-union = '(1 2) '(2 3))                   ; => (1 2 3)
(<? (make-default-comparator) "a" "b")         ; => #t
(call-with-values (lambda () (vector-partition even? #(1 2 3 4)))
  (lambda (v k) (list v k)))                   ; => (#(2 4 1 3) 2)
```

### One binding, two libraries

Twenty names already existed elsewhere: sixteen in `(goscheme fast)`
(`filter`, `take`, `drop`, `take-right`, `drop-right`, `split-at`, `last`,
`iota`, `zip`, `count`, `find`, `list-index`, `delete`, `delete-duplicates`,
`partition`, `any`, `every`), four more in both `(goscheme fast)` and R7RS
(`vector-swap!`, `vector-reverse!`, `vector-binary-search`,
`vector-partition`), and fifteen that R7RS already provides
(`vector-copy`, `vector-map`, `vector-for-each`, ...).  Rather than keep two
implementations that could drift — or worse, disagree depending on which
`import` came last, because a later import shadows an earlier one — every
overlapping name is **one implementation exported from both libraries**, and
the fast procedures were widened where the SRFI specifies more
(`vector-reverse!` takes a range, `vector-binary-search` accepts both a
`less?`-style predicate and SRFI-133's three-valued comparison).

Two behaviour changes follow from that, both in `(goscheme fast)`:

* `any` and `every` are SRFI-1's now: they return the predicate's own value
  (`every` the last one) rather than a boolean, and they accept several lists.
  Code that used them as booleans is unaffected — the value is still true
  exactly when the predicate succeeded — but code that compared the result
  with `#t` is not.
* `vector-partition` returns SRFI-133's two values: a new vector with the
  accepted elements first, and the number accepted.  It used to return two
  vectors (accepted and rejected).

`count` and `list-index` also accept several lists now, as SRFI-1 specifies.

### Documentation

* `docs/srfi/` mirrors `docs/extensions/`: one page per library with the import
  line, every exported name, its arguments, the semantics (for the folds,
  *which* argument order the procedure is called with), the error conditions
  and an example that was actually run.
* `docs/manual/` is a tutorial in nine chapters, English and Chinese: a tour of
  the language, numbers, concurrency, I/O and the operating system, data and
  text, performance, embedding and `goscheme build`, a cookbook, and the
  pitfalls.
* The test that keeps the extension pages honest now covers the SRFI pages too:
  a library that exports a name its page does not mention fails the suite, and
  so does a library with no page at all.

### Tests

2589 assertions in total: 1227 R7RS, 235 regression, 70 concurrency, 42
network, 35 process, 86 data, 43 match, 462 fast, 175 SRFI-1, 47 small SRFI,
73 SRFI-133 and 94 SRFI-128.

Static binaries only, as before (`SHA256SUMS` covers all six); they are
`CGO_ENABLED=0`, so every library is there except `(goscheme ffi)`.

The binaries are **no longer UPX-packed**: they are about 7.5–8 MB instead of
2.8 MB, in exchange for a faster start and no packer in the build.  `make dist`
now takes a couple of seconds rather than minutes, which is what the packing
used to cost.
